Chimiini (Bravanese) noun classes, from the dictionary's own conventions:

Class 1/2: people, animals, animate beings (e.g. muke 'woman' / wake 'women'). The class 1 prefix is full mu- only on monosyllabic stems or stems with an initial consonant cluster (muke, mubli); otherwise it reduces to m- (e.g. m-tooro 'thief').
Class 3/4: inanimate, m-/mu- singular, mi- plural (e.g. muti 'tree' / miti 'trees').
Class 5/6: i- singular (often augmentative), ma- plural (e.g. ijiwe 'stone' / majiwe 'stones').
Class 7/8: chi- singular (often diminutive), z(i)- plural (e.g. chiti 'chair' / ziti 'chairs').
Class 9/10: singular and plural forms are identical (e.g. mbuzi 'goat(s)').
Class 11: l- singular, m-/n- plural (e.g. lkuta 'wall' / nkuta 'walls').
Class 14: u- prefix, abstract states/conditions/qualities, usually no plural (e.g. uvivo 'ripeness').
Class 15: verbal nouns / infinitives, marked with ku- (or kh-/chi- variants) plus a final -a (e.g. kuviva 'to be ripe').

Definiteness ('the X') is marked by a suffix that REPLACES the noun's final vowel, based on what that final vowel is: -a -> -aani, -e -> -eeni, -i -> -iini, -o -> -ooni, -u -> -uuni. Examples: skoola 'school' -> skolaani 'the school', kazi 'work' -> kaziini 'the work', suuqu 'market' -> suuquuni 'the market'.

Possessives ('my/your/his-her/our/their X') agree with the possessed noun's class. For 1st singular, 2nd person, and 3rd singular, the possessive is a SUFFIX attached directly to the noun; for 1st plural and 3rd plural, the possessive is a SEPARATE following word. 1st singular ('my'), suffix -a: class 7 -> cha, class 15 -> ka, class 11 -> la, classes 1/2/3/14 -> wa, classes 4/5/6/9 -> ya, classes 8/10 -> za. 2nd person ('your'), suffix -o: class 7 -> cho, class 15 -> ko, class 11 -> lo, classes 1/2/3/14 -> wo, classes 4/5/6/9 -> yo, classes 8/10 -> zo. 3rd singular ('his/her'), suffix -e: class 7 -> che, classes 15/17 -> ke, class 11 -> le, classes 1/2/3/14 -> we, classes 4/5/6/9 -> ye, classes 8/10 -> ze. 1st plural ('our'), separate word ending in -iitu: classes 1/2/14 -> wiitu, class 9 -> yiitu, classes 8/10 -> ziitu, class 17 (locative, 'place') -> kiitu (following its own k- pattern like ka/ko/ke/kaawo elsewhere, NOT grouped with class 15), all other classes (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 15) -> ndiitu (not the same class-consonant pattern as the other persons -- most classes take the fixed form ndiitu here). kiitu 'our place' and kaawo 'their place' (class 17, locative) can refer to any place -- a house or anywhere else -- not just a home specifically. 3rd plural ('their'), separate word ending in -aawo: class 7 -> chaawo, classes 15/17 -> kaawo, class 11 -> laawo, classes 1/2/3/14 -> waawo, classes 4/5/6/9 -> yaawo, classes 8/10 -> zaawo.

Verb extensions (stack onto the CVC root, roughly extension-causative-reciprocal in order): causative is -ish/-esh (ku-waandra 'get fat' -> ku-waandrisha 'fatten'); stems ending in -uk/-ok mutate the k to sh instead (k-oondroka 'wake up' -> k-oondrosha 'wake s.o. up'). Applied (benefactive/instrumental/directional) is -il/-el, or -iliz/-elez combined with causative. Reciprocal is -an- (ku-'ahidana 'promise one another'), and stacks freely onto applied stems (kh-pikilana 'cook for one another'). A common transitive/causative/intransitive triplet is root+il/el (transitive), root+iz/ez (transitive-causative), root+ik/ek (intransitive); the same pattern recurs as ul/ol, uz/oz, uk/ok, with vowel harmony (high i/u vs mid e/o) picked by the root's final vowel. Some Somali-derived roots take a semantically-empty -at- extension directly on the root.

Tense/mood is built from subject-prefix + auxiliary/marker + stem, not just a past-tense suffix: infinitive is ku-stem-a (becomes kh- before a voiceless-obstruent-initial stem, is dropped before a stem already starting kh-/q-, and lengthens/merges with a vowel-initial stem, e.g. k-aala 'to plant'). Affirmative habitual is invariant hu-stem-a with no subject agreement (hu-biga 'x hits'). The chi- subject prefix marks 3rd person narrative/continuous past in storytelling. Ordinary past tense commonly ends in an -ile/-iile suffix on the verb stem. Negative tenses use a distinct negative subject-prefix set that varies by tense (present, past, future, habitual, imperative, subjunctive each have their own negative paradigm). The copula is irregular: present ni (affirmative) / siwo (negative), invariant; future is SubjectPrefix-taa-ku-wa; past is SubjectPrefix-waaliko. Possession ('have') uses SubjectPrefix-na-cho/na-ye/etc. + the possessed noun, not a separate verb.

Separate from that, there is a LOCATIVE copula ('to be at/in/on [a place]'), built from the root -ko, with a -pi suffix added for 'where' questions. Attested forms -- note several are homophonous across person/class, so context or an explicit subject is needed to disambiguate: 1st singular: niiko 'I am at' (negative siiko 'I am not at'). 2nd singular: uko 'you are at' (homophonous with 3rd singular). 3rd singular (person): uko 'he/she is at' (negative ntaako). 1st plural: chiiko 'we are at' (negative ntachiiko; where-question chikopi 'where are we'; homophonous with the class 7 form below). 2nd plural: niiko 'you (pl.) are at' (homophonous with 1st singular; where-question niikopi 'where are you (pl.)'). 3rd plural (people): waako 'they are at' (negative ntawaako; where-question waakopi 'where are they'). Noun-class locative forms ('it/they [class] is/are at'): class 3 -> wiiko/wuuko (where-question wuukopi); class 4/6 -> yaako (where-question yaakopi); class 5/9 -> yiiko (where-question yiikopi); class 7 -> chiiko (negative ntachiiko; homophonous with 1st plural above); class 8/10 -> ziiko (where-question ziikopi); class 11 -> liiko (where-question liikopi).
These are general patterns, not exhaustive rules -- prefer the specific lexicon entries and example sentences provided below over these generalizations whenever they conflict.
